Na₂HPO₄ (disodium hydrogen phosphate) and KH₂PO₄ (potassium dihydrogen phosphate) are both phosphate salts used in chemistry. When combined in specific ratios, they form what's known as a phosphate buffer system.

A buffer solution is a mixture that can resist changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added. This property is crucial in many biological and chemical applications where maintaining a stable pH is important.

In this case:
- Na₂HPO₄ acts as a weak base (the conjugate base in the buffer system)
- KH₂PO₄ acts as a weak acid (the conjugate acid in the buffer system)

The pH of 7.4 mentioned in the problem is physiological pH (slightly alkaline), which is the normal pH of human blood and many bodily fluids. This pH is maintained by the proper ratio of these two components.

The fact that the solution has a precise pH of 7.4 indicates that these chemicals are being used to create a buffered solution that will maintain this pH even when other components are added.

Looking at the options:
A. Make a buffered solution - This matches our analysis
B. Make a neutral solution - No, pH 7.4 is slightly alkaline, not neutral (pH 7.0)
C. Make a very acidic solution - No, pH 7.4 is slightly alkaline
D. Make a very alkaline solution - No, pH 7.4 is only slightly alkaline, not "very alkaline"

The correct answer is A. Make a buffered solution.
